newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Stals says better BoP to aid fx control removal.
newsitem.headline: Stals says better BoP to aid fx control removal.

text.p: Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday that an improved balance of payments in 1997 would help government in its decision on removing remaining foreign exchange controls.
"The Reserve Bank will continue to advise the government on further foreign exchange control relaxations," Stals told reporters at a media briefing in Cape Town.
"That will of course be facilitated by the expected further improvement in the underlying balance of payments in 1997," he said.
Stals said, however, that the central bank would move with caution in the advice that it gave to government on the gradual removal of controls.
"We cannot just remove all exchange controls in a big bang approach for as long as the country's capacity for converting rand assets into foreign currencies is extremely limited," he said.
"The bank must therefore move with caution and discretion in the advice it gives to government for the gradual removal of the remaining exchange controls," he added.

Commenting on the rand's recent strength, Stals said its appreciation in January had been a welcome development which would help in the central bank's aim to bring inflation below 10 percent for the year.
The rand has firmed more than five percent against the dollar since the beginning of the year.
Monetary authorities remain concerned, however, about the danger of a further rise in the rate of inflation, Stals said.
"An overaccomodative monetary policy at this stage would be very dangerous," he added
He said the Bank would first wait for more convincing evidence that bank credit extension and money supply were being reined in before moving to ease its monetary policy.

"The Reserve Bank will first...want to see more convincing evidence that the rates of increase of bank credit extension and in the money supply will decline to a more acceptable level before supporting any relaxation of the existing restrictive monetary policy measures," he said.

Credit extension to the private sector grew at a rate of 15.75 percent in December compared with 17.13 percent in November, while money supply growth rose a preliminary 13.73 percent from 15.32 percent.

Stals said the decrease in credit extension and money supply were, however, tentative signs that underlying conditions in both the real economy and the financial markets had begun to improve after October last year.

Other visible changes included a slowdown in the rate of increase in gross domestic expenditure, a substantial improvement in the current account of the balance of payments and reduced pressure on the rand.

"Market fundamentals therefore changed for the better and now, the beginning of 1997, there is a lot of optimism that 1997 will provide a return to overall financial stability for the South African economy," Stals said.
